articles.title: Commonwealth medallist Lobban switches from Scotland to Australia
articles.summary: Scottish-born squash player Greg Lobban will represent Australia for the first time at this week's China Open.
articles.body:
Scottish-born squash player Greg Lobban will represent Australia for the first time at this week's China Open.

The 34-year-old, who was born in Inverness and has represented Scotland at three Commonwealth Games, confirmed his Australian citizenship had been approved on Tuesday, saying he will now "get to play under the Australian flag".

Lobban won a doubles bronze medal for Scotland at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and has 16 PSA titles to his name.

The news is therefore a blow to Scottish squash but does not come as a surprise.

In an interview with BBC Scotland in June, the world number 29 confirmed he was in the process of applying for citizenship in Australia and believed it was "the best decision for me and my family".

Lobban, who has an Australian wife, added that the lure of potentially playing at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles - where the sport will make its Games debut - hastened an already planned move.

"I have got strong Australian ties with my wife being born there and my son being half Australian, so this was going to happen at some point," he said.

"I was thinking it was probably going to be post-squash career in terms of applying for residency and citizenship, but the prospect of representing Australia at the Olympics is too much of an exciting opportunity to turn down.

"At this stage of my career, this is really motivation to put in a good two years and hopefully be able to have Australian representation at the Games."

articles.title: La natación española sale a flote
articles.standfirst: Un abanico de nadadores interesantes rodean al contrastado Hugo González. Los inminentes Mundiales de Pekín en piscina corta serán un buen test
articles.summary: Un abanico de nadadores interesantes rodean al contrastado Hugo González. Los inminentes Mundiales de Pekín en piscina corta serán un buen test
articles.body: Pocos deportes en España han transitado su historia internacional por un desfiladero tan estrecho como la natación, donde el talento ha brotado con cuentagotas y cada generación ha tenido casi siempre un único referente al que mirar. A Martin López Zubero, le sucedieron Sergi López, el hermano del primero, David y Nina Zhivaneskaia para desembocar en Mireia Belmonte, la más laureada de todos los mencionados. De pronto apareció Hugo González, un campeón mundial contrastado que aún persigue una medalla olímpica, y parecía que la raquítica hilera avanzaría un periodo más, pero sorprendentemente la última generación que ha surgido hace mirar con optimismo Los Ángeles 2028, el horizonte que fijó Sean Kelley, el antiguo director técnico, cuando tomó las riendas de la natación española tras Tokio 2020. Los Europeos de París del año pasado, el título de 200 braza mundial logrado por un superespecialista en piscina de 25 metros, Carles Coll, en 2024 y los resultados de los Campeonatos de España de la semana pasada han provocado un estado de cierto optimismo que pasa no tantos por los podios, que podría haberlos, como que las tardes de las grandes competiciones tengan banderas españolas en alguna de las ocho calles de las finales. Además de Hugo, que arrojó la segunda mejor marca de 2026 en 200 espalda, es muy valorable lo que aportan Luca Hoek, el velocista más rápido que ha tenido este país, y su compañero de entrenamientos Miguel Pérez-Godoy, ilusionantes si César Castro llega fino a Pekín en dos semanas como el cuarto relevista del 4x200. En un deporte en el que se trabajaba de forma poco transversal, con tipos tan brillantes y tan particulares al mismo tiempo como Fred Vergnoux, ahora parece haber una comunión más clara entre Titley, Greenwood, Navalón... También el sector femenino parece tener una estrella emergente en Irene Ciércoles. Tiene 16 años y es una nadadora por hacer. Pero cada vez que se tira a la piscina, tiembla una plusmarca nacional. Los próximos Mundiales en piscina olímpica de este verano en Budapest se antojan el gran termómetro del estado real de la natación. Pero, de momento, este deporte ha vuelto a los titulares.

articles.title: Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades
articles.summary: People know Josh Kerr the athlete. But are there two Josh Kerrs? The mile world record holder talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, 4am kebabs in Paris, entering races under a false name and his granny keeping him humble.
articles.body:
The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks.

That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record. Then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship.

Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is.

There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably-niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, 4am kebabs in Paris, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble.

This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name, and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation.

The Kerr who is still a regular visitor to first club Edinburgh AC's training sessions. This is Uncle Josh, who is heading for a party with his nephews after this chat.

The difference between the two versions of Kerr? The shades...

"They really help me switch my personality into work mode," he tells BBC Sport. "I think everyone has a work persona and it's a bit more intensified when it comes to my sport.

"Not a lot of things matter when I'm focused on my job, but the rest of the 23 hours and 56-and-a-bit minutes of the day, it's very different."

Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades

'My brother still thinks he can beat me... that's the Kerr delusion'

Kerr is sitting in the bay window of his parents' dining room as the autumnal gloom gathers in this desirable part of Edinburgh. All grand facades, imposing trees and permit parking.

His granny lives at the end of the road. His brother Jake and his family are 20 minutes outside the city. His school – the prestigious George Watson's – is a mile away.

The house has been home since Josh was five months old. Even now, this is where he returns on his five or six trips back to Scotland each year from his Albuquerque base, albeit the "chaos" of his teenage bedroom has long since been vanquished.

"It brings all different sorts of emotions," Kerr says of walking back through the terraced property's teal front door at the start of each visit. "As a kid, I would train from here every day. Everything started from that door.

"It's nice to fall back into that routine when I'm here. I can see the splits I'm running in my loops versus when I was 15. Slightly quicker..."

Around him in the room, pictures of the two brothers fight for space with memorabilia from their careers and assorted artwork. Jake - like their father John - was a professional rugby player, earning a cap for Scotland in the 2019 Six Nations.

He is 18 months older so served as not just an example to follow, but also a target to catch when Josh started racing at the age of nine, having caught the eye at a summer camp.

"If anyone ever wants to nerd out on the family stats, Jake has a pretty awesome under-15 cross-country record," Kerr says.

"We raced a couple of times, once at the Scottish cross-country relays when I ran under someone else's name because they didn't turn up, which was very hush-hush. I just followed him around, holding on for dear life.

"He still likes to remind me that I've never had an unbeaten season and he has. He still thinks he can beat me. That's the solid Kerr delusion in him. But it got me this far, so I can't question it."

The 29-year-old hasn't always had that familial brashness, though.

Dad John says "you wouldn't believe how quiet he was" as a child, speculating that Jake did his talking for him. And mum Jill – who has a background in tennis and is now her son's lead physio – recalls his "kindness and emotional intelligence".

Like all good parents, they are also a source of more esoteric anecdotes. Jill remembers providing both boys breakfasts in bed on competition days and teasing Josh for his "showboating", while John reveals that the teenager turned up to parties with non-alcoholic booze or arrived home sweating if he did have a beer, having run all the way back.

"Those are pretty niche stories," Kerr says, perhaps making a mental note to clamp his father later. "Everyone was starting to get into beers and things like that but it was just not really my thing. I found you could just rip the non-alcoholic bit off the label and get on with the socialising."

By the stage, any ambitions of following his dad and brother into rugby – as a full-back in his case - had been shelved, and his attention focused on athletics.

Kerr "wasn't a phenom by any means" and recalls winning races only "now and again", but the quiet kid had developed a resolve that running would be his future.

"Someone's got to be the best in the world, so why not me? That's what I had in my head," he explains. "I wanted to be a pro athlete and I knew running was going to be my ticket to that. The next stage for me was to go university and get that paid for."

The problem was his athletic record, while good, wasn't stellar. And neither were his academic grades. Kerr needed to hustle.

He enlisted the help of his parents – and fellow Edinburgh AC luminary Chris O'Hare – to compile a list of US colleges and compose a CV and cover letter, then set about selling himself.

"I was 16 and just whipping emails out, left, right and centre, saying 'hey, I'm coming over in 2015, do you have a spot for me?' And it was a pretty big no across the board," says Kerr, who re-read all the rejection emails recently.

"Then New Mexico said 'we'll take you' and I was like, 'perfect, I'll be there'. I told my parents and their first question was 'are they going to pay your fees?' and I was like 'uhm, well, I didn't ask'. So they made me phone back and check!"

He did and they were, which set in motion the move that would change Kerr's life in more ways than one.

It was on his first week in Albuquerque, while on a campus bus that his parents blagged their way on to posing as professors, that Kerr met Larimar Rodriguez, who became his wife last year.

"It was a big week," he says. "It's one of those ones where you don't really realise until you look back.

"I met Larimar when I was 17 and I'm incredibly proud of her. She's done four years of undergrad, four years of med school, and now she's in her fourth year of residency. She'll be a full attending dermatologist by June or July."

Saturday scrap ends with emotional Kerr winning fight

Selfies, signatures & social media - how Kerr embraced Glasgow Games

Britain's Kerr breaks 27-year mile world record in London

'I got recognised at the end of the street... it was my granny'

Josh and Larimar live together in New Mexico with their mini schnauzer El Presidente, who often joins Kerr on his lighter runs.

That's part of a precisely-honed routine that starts with alternate ice baths and hot tub dips at 5am, and some visualisation and journaling around breakfast before he "goes to work" at the track or in the gym from 10am-2pm.

The next three hours are spent in his bedroom, which has been adapted to serve as an altitude chamber, before he retires for the day before 9pm.

The attention to detail is startling. Childhood friend and fellow former world 1500m champion Jake Wightman recounts sharing a room with bronze medallist Kerr at the Tokyo Olympics and looking on in bemusement as he unpacked a scented diffuser, mattress topper and waffle maker to replicate being at home.

Five years on, Kerr has a team of 16 in his Brooks Beast running family under head coach Danny Mackey, including personal chef Jameel, a mental performance consultant and a chiropractor.

It's a long way from life behind that teal door in Edinburgh but how different is Kerr now from the one who left his homeland 11 years ago? "Pretty similar," he says, while acknowledging that he is now more outwardly confident of his abilities.

That "abrasive, calling-your-shot side" as he calls it, is not a traditional trait for a Scot but has been shaped by more than a decade in the United States and by his desire to shine a light on athletics.

"Everyone says, 'oh, we're not getting attention' but go out and earn it," Kerr says. "Make people want to care about what you're doing.

"I'm an individual business and I'm trying as hard as I can to bring eyeballs because I think athletics is the purest form of sport. It didn't really come naturally to me before - being in the US has kind of shaped me a little bit – but I hope people realise that the reason I'm in this position is the blood that runs through my veins.

"I'm able to represent the UK a lot more than I'm able to represent Scotland, but it's such a huge part of who I am. And I hope they take great pride in the performances I'm able to produce.

"I've been inspired by some incredible athletes and I guess this is my turn to step up and try and bridge the gap between grassroots and where I'm at."

Kerr has done that on the track, with two Olympic medals to add to his world indoor and outdoor golds, but he is approaching a stage where his celebrity might breach the confines of athletics.

Take last week. On a four-day visit home, his duties as Uncle Josh were surrounded by a glut of sponsorship and media engagements – including an appearance on the BBC's flagship current affairs programme Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg - as well as a coaching session with young athletes and an invite to carry out the match ball at Murrayfield before Scotland faced New Zealand.

Of course, the omnipresent spectre of BBC Sports Personality of the Year is looming into view, too. Kerr, it should be noted, is not shy in coveting that prize.

That he will likely be one of the main contenders speaks to how life has changed for him in the past couple of years.

Kerr can still enjoy being back in Edinburgh in relative peace - "I got recognised at the end of the street recently… it was my granny" – but concedes life in America can be a bit more challenge because of requests for "400 selfies and a video for their nan".

That attention will only intensify over the coming months should he complete the one or two outstanding items on his athletics tick list and frank his ambition of being "remembered as the best middle-distance athlete of all time".

While he is waiting to see how his winter training goes before 'calling his shot' again, Kerr has other world records in his sights and, of course, Los Angeles in 2028 and a chance to complete the full set of Olympic medals by winning gold.

Silver was not what he wanted in Paris - albeit the passing of time has allowed some satisfaction with the British record he ran – so righting that wrong in the States is top of his agenda.

Kerr has already made a low-key visit to the Colosseum, the epic venue two hours from his New Mexico home where the athletics events will be staged, to help visualise the moment – just as he did with the Stade de France.

He will be back again before the shades go on and he gets down to the business of proving himself to be the best ever.

articles.title: 'You cannot be a champion without working like one': Vivaan Kapoor on his Doha silver, Olympic dream
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: For shooter Vivaan Kapoor, winning a silver medal at the World Championships in Doha in the men's trap event was not just a reward for his hard
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For shooter Vivaan Kapoor, winning a silver medal at the World Championships in Doha in the men's trap event was not just a reward for his hard work but also a reminder of how far he has come in a sport where one missed target can change everything. Having secured an Olympic quota for India, the young shooter is now focused on maintaining his form, making the most of the opportunities ahead and continuing his journey towards the biggest stage in sport."It was not easy because it was a very windy time when we went there. There were a lot of gusts of wind and even the second day was very gloomy. In shooting, especially in my event, it really matters whether it is cloudy or sunny because that depends on how you see the target," Kapoor said.However, he believes that dealing with such challenges is part of an athlete's preparation. "Wind is generally the toughest thing to keep control of. But in the end, it was the same for everybody. We train to be in such conditions and perform even when things are tough," he said.While technical ability remains central to shooting, Kapoor believes the mental side of the sport is what separates the best from the rest. With several shots to negotiate in quick succession, the ability to move on from a mistake can be the difference between a medal and a disappointing finish.For Kapoor, the key word is 'reset'."You cannot be a superhuman or a robot. It is normal to feel bad after missing a target. I tell myself, 'Okay, Vivaan, you are feeling bad about it. See what you did, try not to make that mistake the next time and move forward.' You don't have much time before your next shot, so you cannot get into a deep analysis. You have to understand the mistake and move on," he explained.He believes that champions are often distinguished by how quickly they can put a bad shot behind them rather than by whether they experience disappointment at all.Kapoor's recent progress has also been shaped by technical changes. Around six months ago, he decided to change his personal coach and began working with Croatian shooter Giovanni Cernogoraz, an Olympic gold medallist."The changes were made collectively by my personal coach and national coach. Peter Wilson helped me change my stance, while my stock was also changed. There were a few things related to my movement towards the target that we worked on. Making these changes in such a short time before the World Championships was challenging, but when you make the right changes, things start going up," he said.The 24-year-old also credited the changing atmosphere within the Indian shooting camp for the country's growing success on the international stage. He believes Wilson has brought a different mindset to the team, encouraging shooters to embrace pressure rather than be overwhelmed by it."I think 65 per cent of this sport is mental, and the biggest change has been the mental approach brought in by Peter Wilson. The enthusiasm he brings is unbelievable. We did not have anybody with us who had such great ambitions for the country. He teaches us to shout 'India' loudly in the hotel. Earlier, we were shy about these things," Kapoor said.He added that the emphasis was now on believing that Indian shooters could dominate at the highest level."You can crumble under pressure or embrace it as a privilege. You can tell yourself that this is why you are here and why you do this sport for a living. That change in mood and mentality has been a big thing for us."Kapoor's own journey into shooting began through his father, who would occasionally visit shooting ranges with his friends. Although there were no shooters in his family, the stories he heard at home sparked an early fascination with firearms.Professionally, he drew inspiration from several coaches and accomplished shooters. He particularly remembers former coach Mansher Singh for instilling discipline during his formative years and Khalid Al-Mudaf for helping him develop the mental side of the sport. He also spoke warmly about Kainan, whom he considers an important influence in his development.However, it is his current coach Cernogoraz's work ethic that has left a lasting impression."He is somebody I look up to in terms of working hard. I realised that you cannot be a champion without working like a champion. I am fortunate to see how he works, from morning to evening at the range, and then comes back and runs 10 kilometres. When you see someone like that, it motivates you," Kapoor said.With the Los Angeles Olympics now on the horizon, Kapoor is keen to keep his feet on the ground. While his performance in Doha secured an Olympic quota place for India, it does not automatically guarantee him a place in the final team. The country's selection process will involve domestic trials, making the coming competitions equally important."By God's grace, I have the points and I am going to follow a plan that I had already made," he said.He is now looking forward to domestic competitions before assessing his international schedule and possible World Cup appearances.For a shooter who has learnt to put a missed target behind him and focus on the next one, the approach towards Los Angeles remains much the same. There is no room to dwell on what could have been in Doha or get carried away by what lies ahead. As Kapoor puts it, his job is to pick up his gun every day, give his best and enjoy the sport.And perhaps that is the mindset that will define the next chapter of his journey — one target at a time, with Los Angeles firmly in sight.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Athletics 2026 Season In Review: Andy Ibañez
articles.body:
It's that time of the year again! Athletics Nation is set to begin our annual Player Review Series. We'll be taking a look back at all the different players that suited up for the Green & Gold this year. Some were major contributors while others barely made any impact. Either way, we'll take a look back at the guys that made up the 2026 Athletics. We kick things off with infielder Andy Ibañez, who made the Opening Day roster after a late addition but wouldn't last long with the organization.

The Athletics claimed Ibañez off of waivers from the Los Angeles Dodgers on February 6th, less than a week before pitchers and catchers were due to report. Los Angeles had given Ibañez a relatively large $1.2 million contract earlier in the offseason with the hope that his salary would be too much to stomach for a claiming team. Since he was out of options, if Los Angeles decided to try to sneak him through waivers they could lose him to another team if that team were willing to take on that contract. Los Angeles went that route, trying to stash him in the minors as an expensive backup. The A's called the Dodgers' bluff and added him to the roster, along with the $1.2 million to the payroll.

The former Cuba defector has been around for a few years now. Ibañez made his big league debut in 2021 for the Texas Rangers at the age of 28. The right-handed hitter had a solid rookie campaign but would find himself in Detroit less than two years later. Those three years he spent with the Tigers were also productive as he was a multi-positional Swiss army knife for two playoff teams.

Still, it's not like he was lighting up the world on fire in the batter's box after slashing .239/.301/.352 in his final year in Detroit. Mostly a second and third baseman, the hope when the A's added him to the roster was that he could act as a safeguard at two questionable positions, primarily third base. Max Muncy was about to begin his first full season as a big leaguer at the hot corner and Ibañez could be the veteran fallback option if the former first-rounder couldn't figure it out. He wouldn't provide much upside, but even league-average production would be an upgrade over the previous year.

While Ibañez managed to hold onto a roster spot for the first 28 games, he only ended up getting into 11 of those contests for the Green & Gold with 18 plate appearances. He didn't make the most of those at bats as he collected just two singles and a walk. It wasn't what the A's were looking for, and with Muncy getting everyday at bats at the hot corner the A's elected to designate Ibañez for assignment on April 26th.

He was claimed off waivers by the New York Mets a few days later, taking on the remainder of his salary for the year. That was nice for the A's to get out of that contract. Ibañez made it into three games for New York but then spent the rest of the year in the minors, mostly with the Mets' Triple-A affiliate and then a brief stint in Seattle's system to end the year. Overall he went just two-for-23 in the big leagues this year while slashing .291/.325/.425 with 7 home runs in the minors.

Ibañez now finds himself back on the free agent market after electing free agency on November 2nd. He'll have to settle for a minor league deal wherever he can get one, but with his versatility on defense he should be able to find someone who would be interested in a depth piece like him. It just likely won't be the A's.

And so it begins. We'll be continuing our Player Review Series tomorrow!

articles.title: Sudáfrica pide disculpas a su mayor leyenda olímpica que competirá por Países Bajos: "Si pudiera, los despediría a todos"
articles.standfirst: El ministro de Deportes abrirá una investigación de las causas que han llevado a la nadadora Tatjana Smith a defender la bandera del país europeo del que también tiene la nacionalidad
articles.summary: El ministro de Deportes abrirá una investigación de las causas que han llevado a la nadadora Tatjana Smith a defender la bandera del país europeo del que también tiene la nacionalidad
articles.body: El ministro de Deportes de Sudáfrica, Gayton McKenzie, ordenó abrir una investigación sobre el trato recibido a la doble campeona olímpica de natación Tatjana Smith, quien anunció recientemente que competirá bajo la bandera de Países Bajos tras denunciar reiterados conflictos con la federación sudafricana. La decisión llegó después de quejas contra los dirigentes de Natación Sudáfrica por retenerle durante doce meses 35.000 dólares en premios que ganó en el Mundial de Natación de Fukuoka (Japón) en 2023. Según recogen medios locales este miércoles, la nadador denunció que el organismo le abonó la suma un año después sin los intereses correspondientes, los cuales solo cobró tras recurrir a sus abogados. El ministro McKenzie pidió disculpas públicas a la nadadora durante una rueda de prensa por el maltrato institucional al considerar: "la han tratado de la peor manera posible. Deberían sentir vergüenza. A Tatjana la han tratado como a una enemiga de este país", añadió. El titular de Deportes solicitó formalmente a la Confederación Deportiva y Comité Olímpico Sudafricano (SASCOC) que inicie una pesquisa contra los directivos de la federación nacional. "Si pudiera, saldría ahí mismo y los despediría a todos de inmediato. Así es como me siento", sumó el funcionario, aunque aclaró que una intervención directa del Gobierno acarrearía una suspensión internacional por parte de World Aquatics —la federación internacional de natación reconocida por el Comité Olímpico Internacional (COI)— y que la ley exige que el caso pase primero por SASCOC. "Si así es como tratan a la mayor deportista olímpica de nuestra historia, ¿cómo estamos tratando a nuestras estrellas emergentes? ¿Qué mensaje le envía todo esto a cada joven nadador sobre lo que puede esperar si nada cambia?", cerró McKenzie. Smith —quien compitió bajo su apellido de soltera, Schoenmaker, antes de contraer matrimonio— posee doble nacionalidad y es la deportista olímpica más laureada en la historia de Sudáfrica con cuatro medallas (dos de oro y dos de plata). La campeona se había retirado en 2024, pero este año revirtió su decisión con la mira puesta en los Juegos Olímpicos de Los Ángeles 2028. Tras conquistar el oro en los 200 metros braza en Tokio 2020 y en los 100 metros braza en París 2024, la nadadora buscará ahora el título en los 50 metros braza representando a Países Bajos. "Para Sudáfrica: cuando era niña, mi mayor sueño era representar a mi país en los Juegos Olímpicos. Pude vivir ese sueño y me dio más de lo que jamás hubiera imaginado", expresó Smith entre lágrimas en un video publicado este mes en sus redes sociales para comunicar su cambio de federación. La nadadora agregó que competir por el equipo neerlandés le permite "explorar otra parte" de su identidad y herencia familiar, además de ofrecerle "un mayor respaldo de alto rendimiento y la posibilidad de construir una carrera más sostenible".

images.caption: Tatjana Smith celebra tras ganar la final de los 100 metros braza en los Juegos Olímpicos de París. LAPRESSE

articles.title: Luke Carson: Rhys McClenaghan's coach steps back from high performance role
articles.summary: Luke Carson, who helped guide Rhys McClenaghan to Olympic gold in 2024, has stepped away from high performance coaching.
articles.body:
Luke Carson, who helped guide Rhys McClenaghan to Olympic gold in 2024, has stepped away from high performance coaching.

It brings an end to one of the most successful athlete-coach partnerships in the history of Irish sport after 12 years together.

Carson, a former gymnast, helped assist McClenaghan to Olympic gold on the pommel horse at the 2024 Games in Paris in what was Ireland's first gymnastics medal.

Together, they completed gymnastics' 'Grand Slam'. McClenaghan, 27, also won back-to-back World Championship golds, as well as three European and a Commonwealth title on top of their Olympic success.

Carson has parted company with Gymnastics Ireland, where he was high performance coach and in charge of the Olympic programme for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

After meeting McClenaghan as a teenager in 2014, Carson said he had "raw talent" and they immediately had a "common understanding" that they would leave "no stone unturned".

Carson explained: "I guess our strategy was to do so much volume it would be unreasonable not to succeed.

"Rhys and I developed a uniquely wonderful dynamic, which was built on mutual respect for one another and for the sport itself.

"By almost every definition we were trailblazers. There was no established system for us to follow, no blueprint to copy, no history of results to soak in.

"Instead we had to create them. We had to dream things that never were."

McClenaghan wins pommel horse gold at Olympics

McClenaghan 2.0 'a work in progress' after injuries

Carson started working with a teenage McClenaghan in 2014 and together they rewrote the history books for Irish gymnastics.

McClenaghan won gold for Northern Ireland at the 2018 Commonwealth Games, and then won the first of his three European titles later that year - a feat he would also repeat in 2023 and 2024.

After a disappointing showing at the delayed Tokyo Olympics in 2021, the Newtownards gymnast bounced back to win back-to-back World Championships in 2022 and 2023.

The peak of their time together came the following year in Paris, when McClenaghan won Olympic gold with a superb routine in the final.

Carson added that their achievements together "once seemed impossible" and became a reality.

"Now that this chapter is coming to a close I can finally look back with an enormous sense of pride and recognise the magnitude of what was achieved and really against all odds.

"I'm incredibly grateful to everybody who supported me throughout this extraordinary journey."

Gymnastics Ireland confirmed to BBC Sport in a statement that Carson was no longer working with the sport's national body in Ireland, and it thanked him "for his hard work and dedication" in the role.

"We are incredibly proud of the achievements delivered through our working relationship with Luke over the past 10 years," Gymnastics Ireland said.

"The most notable of which being Rhys McClenaghan's historic gold in Paris 2024."

After his Olympics success, McClenaghan had surgery on a long-standing shoulder issue and only returned to action in February.

His first major tournament back was the Commonwealth Games in July, when he could only finish in sixth place in Glasgow, and he was seventh at the European Championship final the following month.

At the World Championships in October, without Carson in his corner, McClenaghan missed out on a place in the final as he struggled to regain the form that led him to Olympic gold.

Gymnastics Ireland said that Conor McGovern joined the men's national coaching team and will work alongside national coach Sergey Sizhanov in "guiding our men's programme towards LA 2028 and beyond, with a specific focus on working with Rhys".

Eamon Montgomery and Chester Enriquez have also been based out of Carson's Origin gym and will be impacted by the change.

"As we move forward, working in partnership with Sport Ireland & Sport Northern Ireland, we are excited about the new training program we have put in place in consultation with Rhys & our other LA 2028 potential gymnasts as we head into the Olympic qualification pathway next year," Gymnastics Ireland added.
